g10-civics-uc5-t1.overview: Federalism divides political power between a federal government and regional governments so that each level makes final decisions on some matters. This lesson defines federalism, explains devolution, and shows why coordination between the centre and the regions prevents a monopoly of power.
objectives: Define federalism and identify its two levels of government
Explain the meaning of devolution of power
Describe how power is coordinated between the federal government and the regions
Restate the scholar definitions of federalism in your own words
Explain how federal and regional governments worked together during the Lower Omo flood
g10-civics-uc5-t1.simple: Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a federal government and regional governments. Devolution, the principle behind federalism, transfers power to the regions that make up the federation. Under devolution neither the federal nor the regional government is supreme; power is coordinated between the centre and the regions. This arrangement helps to avoid a monopoly of power because no single body controls everything. Scholars describe federalism as a political organisation in which the activities of government are divided between regional and central governments so that each level makes final decisions on some matters. Federal and regional governments are therefore interdependent rather than mutually exclusive. When the Omo River flooded, the regional state could not cope alone, so the federal government, citizens and religious institutions helped together.
g10-civics-uc5-t1.detailed:
What federalism is. Federalism is a system of government where power is divided between federal and regional governments. The same territory is controlled by two levels of government: an overarching national government responsible for the broader governance of larger territorial areas, and smaller regional governments that govern issues of local concern. Federalism is one of several possible state structures, and it stands between a unitary state, where the centre holds the power, and a confederation, where the member states are clearly dominant.

Devolution and coordination. Devolution is the principle of federalism that means transferring power to the region that constitutes the federation. The devolution of power makes neither the federal nor the regional governments supreme. Instead, power is coordinated between the centre and the region. This arrangement is one mechanism that helps to avoid a monopoly of power, because power is shared rather than concentrated in one hand.

How scholars define it. Different scholars define federalism in different ways. One definition holds that federalism is a political organisation in which the activities of government are divided between regional governments and a central government in such a way that each kind of government has some activities on which it makes final decisions. Another describes it as the advocacy of multi-tiered government combining elements of shared rule and regional self-rule, in which neither the federal nor the constituent units are constitutionally subordinate to the other. A third calls it an institutional arrangement in which public authority is divided between state governments and a central government, each level makes final decisions on some issues, and a high federal court adjudicates disputes concerning federalism.

Shared rule and regional self-rule. In a federation each level has sovereign powers that are derived from the constitution rather than from another level of government. Each is empowered to deal directly with its citizens in the exercise of its legislative, executive and taxing powers, and each is directly elected by its citizens. This combination of shared rule and regional self-rule is the heart of the federal idea: the desire to be united for some purposes and autonomous for others.

The Lower Omo case. A few years ago heavy rain in the highland areas of the Lower Omo Basin made the Omo River overflow its banks. The floods destroyed villages and farm lands, many livestock died, and thousands of people were made homeless. Confronting such a challenge was beyond the capacity of the regional state alone, so the federal government stepped in to help the victims. Ethiopians from different backgrounds responded promptly, religious institutions provided help, and the regional governments mobilised and channelled resources to those affected.

Interdependence, not separation. The Omo flood response showed the role that a coordinated effort of the federal and regional governments can play in solving problems, and it showed a spirit of unity and care for human beings in Ethiopia. It also showed that regional states are interdependent: they are not mutually exclusive units that ignore one another. Federalism divides power, but it also joins the levels of government in a single political community that must work together when a problem exceeds the capacity of one level.

workedExamples.problem: A regional state is struck by a drought that is too severe for its own budget. Explain, using the meaning of federalism, who should act and why.
workedExamples.given: The disaster exceeds the capacity of the regional state; the federal government has broader resources.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: in a federation power is divided but coordinated between the centre and the regions.
workedExamples.substitution: A problem beyond the capacity of one region requires coordinated action by both levels.
workedExamples.calculation: The regional government reports and channels local resources, while the federal government provides additional relief.
workedExamples.answer: Both levels act together; federalism coordinates the centre and the region instead of isolating them.

workedExamples.problem: A citizen argues that because his region has its own government, the federal government has no right to deal with him at all. Is he correct?
workedExamples.given: The citizen lives in a regional state within a federation.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: in a federation each level is empowered to deal directly with its citizens in the exercise of its powers.
workedExamples.substitution: The federal constitution gives each level power to legislate, execute and tax.
workedExamples.calculation: Since both levels derive sovereign powers from the constitution, both may deal with the citizen on the matters assigned to them.
workedExamples.answer: No. Both levels deal directly with citizens within their constitutional powers.

workedExamples.problem: Two neighbours argue about whether the devolution of power to the regions has made the federal government weak. Use the lesson to judge.
workedExamples.given: Devolution transfers power to the regions that make up the federation.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: devolution makes neither level supreme and coordinates power between them.
workedExamples.substitution: The federal government keeps the powers shared in common while regions handle local identity matters.
workedExamples.calculation: Power is redistributed rather than destroyed, so the federal level is not weakened but limited and coordinated.
workedExamples.answer: Devolution does not weaken the federation; it prevents a monopoly of power by coordinating the two levels.

commonMistakes: Thinking that federalism means the regions become completely independent countries.
Believing that in a federation one level of government is supreme over the other.
Confusing a federation with a unitary state in which only the centre holds power.
Assuming that regional governments and the federal government never work together.
Believing that devolution means the centre gives up all of its authority.
Forgetting that each level of government derives its powers from the constitution, not from the other level.
applications: Seeing both the federal government and your regional state fund the schools and health centres near you.
Noticing how federal and regional authorities cooperate when a flood or drought strikes your area.
Explaining to a friend why your regional state can pass its own laws on certain local matters.
Following news of a dispute between the centre and a region that is decided by the federal court.
Taking part in a kebele or woreda meeting, which shows power being exercised below the centre.
g10-civics-uc5-t1.summary: Federalism is a system in which power is divided between a federal government and regional governments, with devolution transferring power to the regions. Neither level is supreme; power is coordinated to avoid a monopoly, and each level holds sovereign powers derived from the constitution and deals directly with citizens. The Lower Omo flood showed that the levels of government are interdependent and must cooperate when a problem exceeds the capacity of one region.

g10-civics-uc5-t2.overview: Federations can be classified in different ways, most importantly as dual federalism, which separates the powers of the levels like the layers of a cake, and cooperative federalism, which mixes them like a marble cake. This lesson explains each type with its advantages and disadvantages.
objectives: Explain how federal systems divide power between the federal government and the states
Contrast a confederal arrangement with a federation
Define dual federalism and explain the layer cake image
Define cooperative federalism and explain the marble cake image
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of each type of federalism
g10-civics-uc5-t2.simple: Federal systems divide power between the federal government and the states. Laws made by the states usually apply only in their own region, while laws made by the federal legislature apply in all states. In a confederal arrangement the central government has no direct authority over the lives of citizens, but in a federation the federal government does have direct authority. Based on how federal governments execute their laws across the whole territory, federations are classified as dual federalism and cooperative federalism. Dual federalism, called layer cake federalism, clearly separates the powers of the two levels, so neither interferes with the other. Cooperative federalism, called marble cake federalism, lets the federal, state and local governments interact and work together to solve common problems. Each type has its own advantages and disadvantages.
g10-civics-uc5-t2.detailed:
Dividing power in a federation. Federal systems are usually known for dividing power between the federal government and the states. Laws that are made by the states or regions usually apply to the respective regions, whereas laws made by the federal legislature apply to all states. In con-federal arrangements the central government has no direct authority over the lives of citizens, but in federations the federal government does have direct authority over citizens by legislating rules and laws. The key issue is how federal governments execute their laws across the whole territory of their country, because the enforcement and coordination of such laws throughout the territory is an essential aspect of building one political and economic community.

Two ways of classifying federations. Based on how federal governments execute their laws across the whole territory, federations can be classified as dual federalism and cooperative federalism. Federations also differ by how they came into being. In coming-together federalism, previously independent units decide to join and form a common federal government, as happened in the United States. In holding-together federalism, a country that already exists as one state restructures itself federally in order to hold its diverse groups together, which is the pattern of Ethiopia.

Dual federalism: the layer cake. Dual federalism is a system that clearly divides government authority between state and national governments, and it is often called layer cake federalism. State governments have their own powers, where the central government could not intervene, and the reverse is also true. Earlier, state governments controlled almost all aspects of individual citizens, while the national government had authority over internal improvements, international relations and the regulation of those relations, and determining commercial aspects between the states. Different states have varying laws on divorce, marriage and speed limits, formed on the basis of each state's own requirements.

Advantages of dual federalism. Dual federalism allows the protection of local jurisdictions from federal government overreach, and it prevents the federal government from having too much power in its hands. It also allows local laws to develop and reflect the requirements and wants of local constituents. For instance, a state that is less populated and less congested might assign a higher speed limit than others.

Disadvantages of dual federalism. Dual federalism ensures that tension between the state and the federal government always stays at the brim, and this rising tension is not favourable for the development and well-being of the state and the country as a whole. The tension also leads to decreasing levels of cooperation between the federal and state governments, which reduces the efficiency of programmes that require full cooperation from both governing bodies. As the power in the hands of the states increases, the unity between the different states tends to decrease.

Cooperative federalism: the marble cake. Cooperative federalism requires state and national governments to share power and collaborate on overlapping functions. An example is the federal government giving tax revenue to the states to fund interstate highways, while the states govern the construction and maintenance process in accordance with goals set by the national government. Also known as marble cake federalism, it is a concept in which federal, state and local governments interact cooperatively and collectively to solve common problems rather than making policies separately but more or less equally.

Advantages and disadvantages of cooperative federalism. Under cooperative federalism the national and state governments work together to provide services efficiently, and it offers a more practical approach to intergovernmental relations as more complex problems arise that cannot be addressed at only one level of government. Both levels keep their own powers and responsibilities, which gives people a sense of participation and prevents either from gaining excessive power. States have an incentive to cooperate and can influence how programmes are implemented. The main disadvantage is a decrease in the powers of the states, because the federal government may intervene in policies once reserved to the states.

workedExamples.answer: The claim is too strong; the best type depends on the country and the problem to be solved.

g10-civics-uc5-t2.summary: Federations divide power between the federal government and the states, and they can be classified in more than one way. Dual federalism separates the two levels like the layers of a cake and protects local jurisdiction, but it breeds tension and weakens unity. Cooperative federalism mixes them like a marble cake so that the levels share and collaborate on overlapping functions, though this reduces the powers of the states. Federations also differ by origin: some come together from independent units and others are held together by restructuring a single state.

g10-civics-uc5-t3.overview: Although federations differ from one another, they share a set of essential features: a constitutional division of power, a decentralised system of government, and a written and supreme federal constitution. This lesson identifies and explains those common features.
objectives: State the main features that federations share
Explain how political power is divided in a federation
Distinguish a decentralised system from a federal system
Explain why a federal constitution must be written and supreme
Describe the role of a rigid constitution and a special judiciary in a federation
g10-civics-uc5-t3.simple: There is difficulty in defining exactly what counts as a federation, because federations change over time and take different forms. Even so, they share common characteristics. The first is the division of power: legislative, executive, judicial and financial powers are constitutionally divided between the federal government and the states, based on the desire to be united for some purposes and autonomous for others. The second is a decentralised system of government, although in a true federation the division of power is constitutionally guaranteed and the states are not creations of the federal government. The third is a written and supreme federal constitution to which both levels must submit. Federations also need a rigid constitution, a special judiciary and separate governments with a bicameral legislature.
g10-civics-uc5-t3.detailed:
The search for common features. There is admittedly difficulty in defining what we mean by federations. Like many concepts and institutions, federations are in a process of change, and the ways they manifest themselves in different polities are far from the same. Nonetheless, many continue to speak and write about federations believing that they share certain common characteristics. By way of summary, the essential features characterising a federal state structure can be listed and explained.

Division of power. No one contends the fact that federations are distinguished from other polities primarily by the fact that political power, commonly related to legislative, executive, judicial and financial functions, is constitutionally divided between the federal government and the states. This is indirectly based on the dual principle implicit in every federation: the desire to be united and to be autonomous. Federations share powerful motives to be united for certain purposes and deep-rooted motives for autonomous states for other purposes. The federal government is often empowered with those powers that are shared in common, and the states are empowered with those powers considered relevant for the expression of regional identity.

Decentralised system of government. As opposed to confederations, in decentralised governments the units, often called local governments, are subordinate to the centre. However wide the powers they may exercise, the local governments are merely creations of the centre by a statute, and as a result they may be wiped out by the centre at any time. The arrangement presupposes the existence of a central authority that may delegate a portion of its authority to the local governments, but such delegation is subject to unilateral withdrawal, amendment or revocation by the centre. In some cases absorbing a local government may be politically unwise even when it is legally possible, but this does not change the theory that they are subject to unilateral revocation. In decentralised systems the emphasis is on self-rule rather than on shared rule.

The federal alternative to mere decentralisation. In a federation, on the other hand, the division of power is constitutionally guaranteed and the states are not creations of the federal government. Both the federal government and the states derive their authority from the federal constitution, and as a result neither level can change the terms of the compact as enshrined in the constitution. This is the essential difference between a decentralised unitary state, where delegated power can be taken back, and a true federation, where power belongs to each level in its own right.

A written and supreme federal constitution. A shared feature of federations is that the division of power between the federal government and the states is based on a written and supreme federal constitution to which both orders of government must submit. Federations originate from particular bargains struck at a particular time and designed to serve for generations, so written constitutions are necessary records of the terms of the bargain. The terms of the agreement that establish the federal government and the states, and that distribute powers between them, must be enshrined in a supreme federal constitution which is binding. This is a logical necessity: if the two levels are to remain autonomous within their own spheres, the authority of one should not depend on the other but must derive from something supreme to both.

Rigid constitution, special judiciary and separate governments. The constitution of a federation should be more or less rigid, because a flexible constitution would allow the central government to curtail the autonomy of the federating states. Because disputes may arise between the centre and the units, or between one unit and another, a special judiciary with wide powers must be established to adjudicate them in the light of the constitution. This court acts as the custodian and guardian of the constitution and may declare any law, national or local, invalid if it is at variance with the constitution. In addition, both the centre and the units have their own separate governmental apparatus, and the Ethiopian constitution provides a bicameral legislature made up of the House of Peoples Representatives and the House of Federation.

keyTerms.def: The constitutional splitting of legislative, executive, judicial and financial power between the federal government and the states.
The collective characteristics of a people that the states are empowered to protect and express.
A system in which local governments are subordinate to the centre and may be revoked by it.
The power of the centre to take back delegated authority on its own decision alone.
The written constitution that binds both the federal government and the states and from which both derive their authority.
A constitution that is difficult or slow to change because of a detailed and lengthy amendment process.
A court with wide powers that adjudicates constitutional disputes and acts as the guardian of the constitution.
A legislature that comprises two houses, as in Ethiopia's House of Peoples Representatives and House of Federation.

workedExamples.problem: A region has broad powers but its local government was created by a statute of the centre and can be dissolved by the centre at any time. Is this a federation?
workedExamples.given: The unit exercises wide powers but is a creation of the centre.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: in a true federation the division of power is constitutionally guaranteed and the states are not creations of the federal government.
workedExamples.substitution: A unit that the centre may wipe out by legislation is a subordinate local government, not a federal state.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the unit is subject to unilateral revocation, it fails the federal test and the system is only decentralised.
workedExamples.answer: No. It is a decentralised system, not a federation.

workedExamples.problem: A national law is passed that conflicts with the federal constitution. What does the special judiciary of a federation do?
workedExamples.given: A law is at variance with the supreme constitution.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the special judiciary is the custodian and guardian of the constitution and may declare invalid any law at variance with it.
workedExamples.substitution: A conflicting law fails the test of conformity with the supreme constitution.
workedExamples.calculation: Applying the constitutional test, the law must be declared invalid, whether it is national or local.
workedExamples.answer: The court declares the law invalid because the constitution is the supreme law.

workedExamples.problem: A federation may be amended by a simple majority of the central parliament whenever it wishes. Explain the problem using the features of federalism.
workedExamples.given: The constitution can be changed easily by the centre alone.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the constitution of a federation should be more or less rigid, since a flexible one lets the centre curtail state autonomy.
workedExamples.substitution: An easily changed constitution lets the centre alter the division of power on its own.
workedExamples.calculation: Without rigidity the states lose constitutional protection, so the arrangement ceases to be a genuine federation.
workedExamples.answer: The constitution must be rigid enough to protect the states from the centre acting alone.

commonMistakes: Thinking that any decentralised system is automatically a federation.
Believing that a federal state derives its authority from the federal government rather than from the constitution.
Assuming the federal constitution can be changed by one level of government alone.
Forgetting that the constitution of a federation must be written, supreme and more or less rigid.
Thinking a special judiciary is optional and that constitutional disputes need no court.
Confusing self-rule with shared rule when describing a decentralised system.
applications: Using the FDRE constitution to see how federal, state and concurrent powers are listed.
Following a case where the House of Federation interprets the constitution and settles a dispute.
Comparing the powers of your regional state council with those of the federal parliament.
Discussing why the constitution must be amended through a special, difficult process.
Explaining to classmates why the same law cannot apply in every region in exactly the same way.
g10-civics-uc5-t3.summary: Federations are difficult to define precisely because they keep changing, but they share essential features. Power is constitutionally divided between the federal government and the states, reflecting the desire to be united and autonomous at the same time. A federation differs from a merely decentralised system because its division of power is constitutionally guaranteed, and it rests on a written, supreme and more or less rigid constitution, a special judiciary to guard it, and separate governments including a bicameral legislature.

g10-civics-uc5-t4.overview: Federalism has clear advantages, such as dividing power, protecting against tyranny and increasing citizen participation, and clear disadvantages, such as conflicts of authority, regionalism and inequalities between states. This lesson compares both sides.
objectives: List the main advantages of a federal form of government
Explain how federalism protects citizens against tyranny
List the main disadvantages of a federal form of government
Explain how federalism can produce inequalities between states
Evaluate a federal arrangement by weighing its advantages against its disadvantages
g10-civics-uc5-t4.simple: Federalism is a form of government that allows more than one central entity to have power. There is a federal government above all others, and smaller localised governments that take control of local and regional issues, so that services can better suit the needs of each area. Its advantages include the division of powers, separate governments, a written constitution, a rigid constitution, a special judiciary, a better understanding of local issues, increased citizen participation, protection against tyranny, and greater efficiency. Its disadvantages include conflict of authority between the levels, regionalism replacing patriotism, a lack of accountability, inequalities between states, and the blockage of national policies by states. Every country must weigh these gains and losses.
g10-civics-uc5-t4.detailed:
What federalism offers. Federalism is a form of government that allows for more than one central entity to have power. This means that there is a federal government which is above all others, and smaller, more localised forms of government that take control of local and regional issues. The idea behind this is to be able to better suit the needs of each area of the country, although some issues certainly arise.

Advantages of structure. In a federal government the powers of administration are divided between the centre and the units, and the constitution may either state what powers the federal authority shall have and leave the remainder to the units, or state what powers the units shall have and leave the remainder to the federal authority. Both the centre and the units have their own separate sets of governmental apparatus, so each has separate legislatures and separate executives. A federal government must also have a written constitution, because a federation is a political partnership of various states and therefore needs a written agreement.

Advantages of a rigid constitution and a special judiciary. The constitution of a federation should be more or less rigid, because it is regarded as a sacred agreement and a flexible constitution would let the central government curtail the autonomy of the federating states. In a federation constitutional disputes may arise between the centre and the units, or between one unit and another, and all such disputes must be adjudicated in the light of the constitution. For this purpose a special judiciary with wide powers must be established to act as the custodian and guardian of the constitution, with power to declare any national or local law invalid if it is at variance with the constitution. The constitution is thus the supreme law in a federation, to which both the centre and the states must adhere.

Advantages for better government. The central government has no true way to understand what issues, demands and changes are needed in every area of the country, and this is why federalism is such a great advantage: the smaller branches of local government are right in the middle of local society and are better suited to deal with problems at the grass roots. Because a dual level of government exists, federalism also increases the level of citizen participation in government decision making at the grass roots.

Advantages of protection and efficiency. One of the most important points of federalism is that dividing power between the national government and the state governments, and spreading national power among three branches that check and balance each other, serves as a deterrent to tyranny and runaway power. Federalism is also more efficient: when some powers are dispersed among the states, states can solve their own problems in the way that works best for them. Trying to have a national solution to every problem, sometimes called the cookie-cutter method of law and policy making, ends up with solutions that are more effective in some states and less effective in others.

Disadvantages of federalism. The biggest problem with two bodies of government in power is the power struggle, because both the central and the state governments intend to assert their power over the other, which at times causes conflict, and a long-term conflict can even create hurdles in national development and prosperity. Federalism promotes smaller levels of government and therefore smaller levels of pride, and it can put one region against another and take away from the patriotic feeling that should be present all over the country. Because responsibility is shared, it becomes easy for one sector to release its responsibility to the other, producing a lack of accountability when something goes wrong. Federalism also allows regional inequalities, for example when education, taxes, health care or welfare are state matters, some states spend far more per capita than others. Finally, states can fight against certain national laws by challenging them in court, by failing to enforce them, or by deliberately obstructing their enforcement.

workedExamples.problem: A citizen asks whether federalism is good or bad. Using the lesson, give a balanced answer.
workedExamples.given: Federalism has nine advantages and several disadvantages.

workedExamples.substitution: Protection against tyranny, participation and efficiency are weighed against conflict, regionalism, weak accountability and inequality.
workedExamples.calculation: Since real gains and real costs both exist, judgement must depend on how well a country manages them.
workedExamples.answer: It is neither simply good nor simply bad; its value depends on how well the gains outweigh the costs.

commonMistakes: Listing only the advantages and ignoring the disadvantages of federalism.
Thinking that federalism guarantees equal services in every region automatically.
Believing that shared responsibility always increases accountability, when it can weaken it.
Assuming regionalism and patriotism always support each other.
Forgetting that the special judiciary guards the constitution rather than the government of the day.
Thinking the cookie-cutter method of national policies works equally well in every area.

Taking part in local elections and community meetings, which federalism encourages.
Noticing differences in services between regions and asking why equalisation is needed.
Trusting courts rather than force when a region and the centre disagree about a law.
Appreciating that power is checked and balanced so that no single body rules alone.
g10-civics-uc5-t4.summary: Federalism allows more than one centre of power so that government can suit local needs. Its advantages include the division of powers, separate governments, a written and rigid constitution, a special judiciary, a better understanding of local issues, more citizen participation, protection against tyranny and greater efficiency. Its disadvantages include conflict of authority, regionalism over patriotism, lack of accountability, inequalities between states and the blockage of national policies by states.

g10-civics-uc5-t5.overview: Ethiopia adopted federalism mainly to reconcile its ethnic diversity with political unity after decades of a highly centralised state. This lesson explains the rationale, the features of Ethiopian federalism, and the challenges it still faces.
objectives: Explain why Ethiopia adopted a federal system
Describe how Ethiopian federalism accommodates diversity
State the constitutional division of federal, state and concurrent powers
Describe the structure of the Ethiopian federal legislature
Identify the challenges facing Ethiopian federalism
g10-civics-uc5-t5.simple: The rationale of federalism in contemporary Ethiopia is primarily the reconciliation of ethnic diversity with political unity. For almost a century Ethiopia was a highly centralised unitary state, despite the many multiethnic groups living within it. The idea of creating a centralised and unified state proved ineffective, and governments used to propagate the slogans of one nation, one government, one country, one language and one religion, which sidelined the virtues of diversity. Since 1995 Ethiopia has implemented a federal system, which the constitution adopted to accommodate the rights, needs, claims and demands of its diverse ethnic groups. The federal features include a constitutional division of powers and a bicameral legislature made up of the House of Peoples Representatives and the House of Federation. Federalism has brought both successes and challenges.
g10-civics-uc5-t5.detailed:
Why Ethiopia adopted federalism. The rationale of federalism in contemporary Ethiopia is primarily the reconciliation of ethnic diversity with political unity. In many ways the present federal system is the culmination of a long period of searching for a constitutional formula which can unite and contain the Ethiopian peoples. Ethiopia has been a country that, for almost a century, experienced a highly centralised unitary state structure, irrespective of the diverse multiethnic groups that exist within the state.

The failure of the centralised past. The idea of creating a centralised and unified Ethiopian state proved to be ineffective. Any viable government structure must be marked by a considerable degree of decentralisation, and federalism could therefore offer a promising formula for a smooth and satisfactory process of unity. The introduction of a federal system was denied attention and recognition during past centuries, as most governments used to propagate the idea of one nation, one government, one country, one nation, one language and one religion. This completely sidelined the virtues of diversity.

Accommodating the interests of ethnic groups. The existing federal arrangement, the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, is devised with the aim of accommodating the interests of distinct ethnic groups in Ethiopia. Federalism is one of the essential elements for accommodating the rights, needs, claims and demands emerging among diverse ethnic groups. The reason Ethiopia has recognised federalism as an essential mechanism in the current constitution is to accommodate its multi-faceted diversity. Ethiopia has been implementing federalism since 1995, with both a great deal of success and challenges.

Feature one: the constitutional division of power. Federalism as a system of government has two levels of government within a state: the state governments and the federal government. The same applies to the Ethiopian federal structure, and in such states a distribution of power between the two levels is a necessary condition, without which the system itself loses its basic essence. The federal constitution regulates inter-government relations and explicitly lists the federal powers, the state powers and the concurrent powers, while leaving residual power to the state. Respect for and mutual non-intervention in each other's powers is also part of the constitution: Article 50(8) declares that federal and state powers are defined by the constitution, that the states shall respect the powers of the federal government, and that the federal government shall likewise respect the powers of the states. Both therefore have a constitutionally limited jurisdiction of power, with the restriction of crossing over into each other's affairs.

Feature two: the bi-cameral legislature. In the case of Ethiopia the constitution provides two federal houses. The House of Peoples Representatives is the supreme political organ in the country, and the House of Federation is the upper house. Article 53(3) states that the highest authority of the federal government rests upon the House of Peoples Representatives, and Article 55 states its powers and functions, beginning with the power to legislate in all matters exhaustively enumerated to the federal government under Article 51. The House of Peoples Representatives, together with the House of Federation, can take appropriate measures on human rights violations that cannot be controlled by any regional state, and it may question the prime minister and other federal officials and, upon the request of one third of its members, discuss any matter pertaining to the power of the executive.

Feature two continued: the House of Federation. The House of Federation is a representative organ whose members represent each nation, nationality and peoples, and it is made up of representatives of nations and nationalities for a tenure of five years. The constitution specifies how many representatives a nationality group shall have: each nationality is represented by at least one member, and larger ethnic groups receive more representation because the provision grants one additional representative for each one million additional population. These members can be elected either directly by the people or indirectly by the state council. The Ethiopian constitution empowers the House of Federation to interpret the constitution.

Challenges to Ethiopian federalism. Federalism is becoming the basis of the political organisation of several states, including Ethiopia, Nigeria, India, Brazil, the United States, Canada, Australia and Germany, although its nature varies from one country to another. Among Ethiopia's peculiar features is the explicit acknowledgement of national self-determination and its firm position to institutionalise the principle, since the constitution defines the right of every group to constitute nations, nationalities and peoples and, rather than recognising only historically mobilised nationalities, prefers a straightforward grant of self-determination to all. One drawback of this approach is that some constituent units have not yet been able to evolve as viable regional governments: some do not seem to have acquired the status of a nation or nationality which the constitution ascribes to them, and have not been able to articulate regional interests worth constituting a federal unit. Lack of experience, skilled manpower and resources and historical marginalisation may have aggravated the problem, but the fact that there is more trouble in some constituent states that have not been historically mobilised calls for some sort of asymmetric federal system, at least in the short run, with the powers of the federal government being extensive in relation to such states.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia was a highly centralised state for nearly a century but contains many multiethnic groups. Explain why this combination pushed the country towards federalism.
workedExamples.given: A centralised unitary structure existed alongside deep ethnic diversity.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the rationale of Ethiopian federalism is the reconciliation of ethnic diversity with political unity.
workedExamples.substitution: Centralised rule proved ineffective and sidelined the virtues of diversity.
workedExamples.calculation: Since unity could not be secured by centralisation alone, a federal formula was adopted to unite and contain the peoples.
workedExamples.answer: Federalism was adopted because centralisation failed to accommodate diversity while preserving unity.

workedExamples.problem: A regional state wants to know which powers belong to it. Using the constitution, explain how the powers are arranged.
workedExamples.given: The federal constitution lists federal powers, state powers and concurrent powers.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: Article 50(8) states that federal and state powers are defined by the constitution and each level must respect the other.
workedExamples.substitution: Enumerated federal powers stay with the centre; enumerated and residual powers stay with the states; concurrent powers are shared.
workedExamples.calculation: Applying the listing, the state may exercise the state and concurrent powers and the residual power left to it, without crossing into federal affairs.
workedExamples.answer: The state holds the listed state powers, shared concurrent powers and residual powers, and must respect federal powers.

workedExamples.problem: A nationality group with a small population claims at least one seat in the House of Federation. Is the claim supported by the constitution?
workedExamples.given: House of Federation seats are allocated among nations, nationalities and peoples.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: each nationality is represented by at least one member, and each additional one million population adds one more representative.
workedExamples.substitution: The minimum guarantee of one member applies to every nationality regardless of size, while larger groups gain extra seats.
workedExamples.calculation: Applying the rule, the small nationality is guaranteed at least one seat and the large group receives more.
workedExamples.answer: Yes. Every nationality is represented by at least one member, and larger groups receive additional representatives.

workedExamples.problem: A constituent state lacks skilled manpower and resources and has not been historically mobilised. What type of federal arrangement does the textbook suggest for such states?
workedExamples.given: Some constituent units have not evolved as viable regional governments.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: such states call for some sort of asymmetric federal system, at least in the short run.
workedExamples.substitution: In relation to weak constituent states, the powers of the federal government need to be extensive compared to those of the regions.
workedExamples.calculation: Applying this reasoning, the federal government should carry more of the burden in those states temporarily.
workedExamples.answer: An asymmetric federal arrangement, with more extensive federal powers for the weaker states in the short run.

commonMistakes: Thinking Ethiopia was always a federal state, when it was centralised for almost a century.
Believing that federalism in Ethiopia exists to divide the country rather than to unite it in diversity.
Confusing the House of Peoples Representatives with the House of Federation.
Assuming that all regional states have equal capacity to serve as viable federal units.
Thinking that one nation, one language slogans protected diversity, when they sidelined it.
Forgetting that the constitution itself acknowledges national self-determination.
applications: Reading the FDRE constitution to see where federal, state and concurrent powers are listed.
Following the House of Federation when it interprets the constitution or settles a dispute.
Taking part in regional and local elections that federal restructuring made possible.
Discussing with classmates how Ethiopian federalism seeks both unity and ethnic self-rule.
Noticing how federal equalisation support helps weaker regional states build capacity.
g10-civics-uc5-t5.summary: Ethiopia adopted federalism to reconcile ethnic diversity with political unity after almost a century of a highly centralised unitary state that sidelined diversity. Since 1995 the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia has listed federal, state and concurrent powers in its constitution, left residual power to the states, and built a bicameral legislature with the House of Peoples Representatives and the House of Federation, which represents every nation, nationality and peoples. Federalism has brought successes but still faces challenges, including constituent states that have not yet become viable regional governments, which calls for asymmetric federal arrangements in the short run.
